column2: and giving them fees and dismissing them, eat with one's kin. Whoever keeps thus the excellent Kamika vow, O brahmin,
gains all desires here and goes to Vishnu's supreme abode. On the eleventh of the bright half of Nabhas, having fasted on the Pavitra,
on the twelfth, disciplined, one should worship Janardana with the sixteen offerings, then feed brahmins,
and giving them fees, one gains a virtuous son here and goes to Vishnu's abode itself, saluted by all the gods.
On the eleventh of the dark half of Nabhasya, having fasted on the one called Aja, one should worship Upendra on the twelfth with various offerings,
feed brahmins with sweet food and dismiss them with fees. Having kept thus with devotion and concentration the vow of Aja, O brahmin,
one enjoys all pleasures here and at the end goes to Vishnu's abode. On the eleventh of the bright half of Nabhasya, having fasted on the one called Padma,
and performed the daily worship there, one should perform the turning ceremony: the image installed earlier, O best of brahmins,
taken in festive procession to a body of water, made to touch the water and duly worshipped there,
should be brought back to the pavilion and laid on its left side. Then at dawn on the twelfth, worshipping Vamana with perfumes and the like,
feeding brahmins and giving fees, one should dismiss them. Whoever keeps the unsurpassed Padma vow thus, O brahmin,
gains enjoyment here and liberation at the end, beyond the world. On the eleventh of the dark half of Isha, having fasted on the Indira,
one should perform shraddha at midday before a shalagrama stone, pleasing to Vishnu, O brahmin; then in the morning on Hari's day
the wise one should worship Padmanabha and feed brahmins, dismiss them with fees, and then eat himself.
A mortal who keeps this vow enjoys desired pleasures here, lifts up a crore of ancestors, and at the end goes to Vishnu's house.
On the eleventh of the bright half of Isha, O brahmin, the one called Papankusha, one should fast duly and worship Vishnu on Vishnu's day;
then feeding the best brahmins and giving them fees, bowing with devotion, one should dismiss them and then eat oneself.
The man who keeps the Papankusha vow thus with devotion enjoys excellent pleasures here and reaches Vishnu's world.
On the eleventh of the dark half of Kartika, O best of brahmins, having duly fasted on the Rama, in the morning of the twelfth one should worship
Keshava, slayer of Keshi, God of gods, eternal; then feed brahmins and dismiss them with fees.
Having kept this vow, O brahmin, enjoying desired pleasures here, one gains nearness to Rama's lord in a celestial car.
On the eleventh of the bright half of Urja, having fasted on the Prabodhini, one should awaken the sleeping Keshava at night with songs and other auspicious things,
with Rig, Yajur and Sama mantras and various instruments, with grapes, sugarcane, pomegranates, bananas, water-chestnuts and the like
as offerings; then, when the night has passed, on the next day, bathing and doing the daily rites, one should worship Damodara with the mace
with the sixteen offerings and the Purusha hymn; feeding brahmins one should dismiss them, pleased with fees,
and then give that golden image with a cow to the teacher. Whoever keeps the Bodhini vow thus with devotion and reverence
enjoys excellent pleasures here and gains Vishnu's abode. On the eleventh of the dark half of Margashirsha, having fasted on the Utpanna,
on the twelfth one should worship Krishna with perfumes and other offerings; then feeding the best brahmins and giving them fees,
dismissing them, one should then eat with loved ones, collected. Whoever keeps the Utpanna vow thus with devotion
mounts a celestial car and at the end goes to Vishnu's abode. On the eleventh of the bright half of Margashirsha, having fasted on the one called Moksha,
in the morning of the twelfth, worshipping Ananta of universal form with all offerings, the brahmin should feed brahmins,
dismiss them with fees and eat with his kin. Having kept this vow, O brahmin, enjoying desired pleasures here,

and lifting up ten generations before and ten after, one goes to Hari. On the eleventh of the dark half of Pausha, having fasted on the Saphala, on the twelfth, worshipping Achyuta with all offerings,
feeding brahmins with sweet food, one should dismiss them with fees. Having kept this vow of Saphala duly, O brahmin,
one enjoys all pleasures here and at the end goes to Vishnu's abode. On the eleventh of the bright half of Pausha, having fasted on the Putrada,
on the twelfth one should worship the discus-bearer with the arghya and other offerings; then feeding the best brahmins and giving them fees,
dismissing them, one should eat the remaining food with one's loved kin. Having kept this vow, O brahmin, enjoying desired pleasures here,
one mounts an excellent celestial car and at the end goes to Hari's temple. On the eleventh of the dark half of Magha, having fasted on the Shattila,
bathing, giving, offering libations, oblations, eating and worship with sesame alone, O best of brahmins, and in the morning of the twelfth,
worshipping Vaikuntha properly with all offerings, one should feed brahmins and dismiss them with fees.
Having kept this vow duly and with concentration, O brahmin, enjoying desired pleasures here, at the end one gains Vishnu's abode.
On the eleventh of the bright half of Magha, having fasted on the one called Jaya, in the morning of Hari's day one should worship the Person, lord of Shri, O brahmin,
feed brahmins, give fees and dismiss them, and then, restrained, eat what remains with one's kin.
Whoever keeps thus the vow that pleases Keshava, O brahmin, enjoys excellent pleasures here and at the end goes to Vishnu's abode.
On the eleventh of the dark half of Tapasya, having fasted on the Vijaya, in the morning of the twelfth, worshipping the lord of yogis with perfumes and the like,
then feeding brahmins and pleasing them with fees, dismissing them, one should eat in silence with one's kin.
A mortal who keeps this vow enjoys desired pleasures here and at the body's end goes to Vishnu's world, well honoured by the gods.
On the eleventh of the bright half of Phalguna, O best of brahmins, having fasted devoutly on the Amalaki, in the morning of the twelfth one should worship
the lotus-eyed one with all offerings, then feed brahmins with excellent food and give them fees.
Having performed the worship of the amalaki and the rest duly on the bright eleventh of Tapasya, one goes to Vishnu's supreme abode.
On the eleventh of the dark half of Chaitra, the Papamochani, O brahmin, having fasted, in the morning of the twelfth one should worship Govinda
with the sixteen offerings, feed brahmins, give them fees, dismiss them and eat with one's kin.
Whoever keeps the Papamochani vow thus, O brahmin, goes to Vishnu's world in a shining celestial car.
Thus the vow of the eleventh, in the dark and bright fortnights alike, is declared to grant liberation, O brahmin; there is no doubt about it at all.
Since it is accomplished over three days and its recital destroys sin, it is to be known as the best of all vows, of great fruit, O brahmin.
One should give up four meals over those three days, O Narada: one each on the first and last, and two on the middle day.
Now I will tell you the rules for this vow over the three days: bronze vessels, meat, lentil food, chickpeas, kodrava,
vegetables, honey, others' food, a second meal and sexual intercourse — these ten things a Vaishnava should always avoid on the tenth.
Gambling, sleep, betel, cleaning the teeth, slander, tale-bearing, theft, violence, lovemaking,
anger and false speech should be avoided on the eleventh. Bronze, meat, liquor, honey, oil, speech with the impure and barbarians,
exercise, travel, a second meal, intercourse, and touching the untouchable — these twelve one should give up on the twelfth.
Keeping these rules, O brahmin, one should observe the fast if able; if unable, the wise one may take one meal, but not only at night,
or live on unasked food; but one should not abandon such a vow.
devoted, with perfumes and the like, feeding the best brahmins with curd-rice, giving a fee of silver, bowing, one should dismiss them:
By this vow may Shridhara, lord of gods, be pleased. On the twelfth of the bright half of Nabhasya the vow-keeper, worshipping Vamana,
should feed twelve brahmins before him with milk-rice, and giving a golden fee, he pleases Vishnu.
On the twelfth of the bright half of Isha one should worship Padmanabha with perfumes and other offerings and feed brahmins before him
with sweet food, and give a golden fee with clothes. Pleased by this vow, Padmanabha, O best of brahmins,
grants going to Shvetadvipa and the bodily pleasures one desires. In the dark half of Kartika is the Govatsa Dvadashi vow:
drawing a cow with its calf there with fragrant substances, worshipping it with sandal and the like and with flower garlands, in a copper
vessel preparing an arghya with flowers, unbroken rice and sesame duly, one should give it at her feet with this mantra, O Narada:

Born of the ocean of milk, saluted by gods and asuras, O Goddess made of all gods, adorned by all gods,
naradapuran:120:31	mother, mother, mother of cows, accept the arghya; salutations to you. Then one should offer vadas made of black gram and the like,
five, ten or one, according to one's means: "Surabhi, you are the mother of the world, ever abiding in Vishnu's abode;
O you made of all gods, eat this mouthful I give. O Goddess made of all gods, adorned by all gods,
mother Nandini, make my wish fruitful." On that day, O best of brahmins, one should avoid food cooked in oil or in a pot,
cow's milk, cow's ghee, curd and buttermilk. On the twelfth of the bright half of Urja, O brahmin, the god Damodara
should be worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, well collected; before him one should feed twelve brahmins with cooked food,
and then lovingly give them pitchers full of water, covered with cloth and worshipped, with betel nut, modakas and gold.
When this is done one becomes dear to Vishnu, enjoying all pleasures, and at the body's end gains union with Vishnu; there is no doubt.
The Nirajana vow is also declared here; learn it from me. At nightfall, adorning the Lord of the world who has risen from sleep,
adorned oneself, producing a new fire and worshipping it with mantras, offering oblations there, when it blazes, with a silver lamp, O sage,
worshipped with perfumes, flowers and the like, the people should wave lights before Hari, and likewise before Lakshmi who follows him, Brahmani, Chandika,
Aditya, Shankara, Gauri, the Yaksha, Ganapati, the planets, the Mothers, the ancestors, the mountains and all the Nagas in order.
One should wave lights before the cows and the herd of buffaloes and the like, with cries of "Salutation! Victory!" and the sound of bells, conches and the like,
with the cows' horns smeared with vermilion and their bodies painted in colours; when the tumult of the cows in the great festival of waving lights is over,
horses with good marks, elephants flowing with ichor, and all the royal insignia, umbrella and the rest, O Narada —
the king, with his priest, attended by ministers and servants, worshipping them duly and himself waving lights with reverence,
amid the sound of conches, trumpets and the like, should sit well adorned on a new throne made of various gems.
Then a courtesan or a woman of good family endowed with good marks should gently wave lights over the king's head.
This great pacification should be performed every year by a king or another wealthy man who desires health for the year.
In whose kingdom, city or village this excellent pacification called Nirajana is performed, O brahmin, their diseases perish.
On the twelfth of the bright half of Margashirsha is the unsurpassed Sadhya vow: Manobhava, Prana, Nara, Yata, Viryavan,
Chiti, Haya, Nripa, Hamsa, Narayana, Vibhu and Prabhu — the twelve Sadhyas are declared.
One should worship these, formed of rice, with perfumes, flowers and the like; then feeding twelve excellent brahmins and giving good fees,
one should dismiss them, saying, "May Narayana be pleased." On this same day is known the vow called Dvadashaditya:
in it the wise one should worship the twelve Adityas — Dhata, Mitra, Aryaman, Pusha, Shakra, Amsha, Varuna, Bhaga,
Tvashta, Vivasvan, Savita and Vishnu are declared the twelve. Worshipping them carefully on the bright twelfth each month,
one should complete the year; at the end of the vow, duly worshipping twelve golden images and feeding the best brahmins,
honouring them well with sweet food, the vow-keeper should give one to each. A man who keeps this vow called Dvadashaditya
reaches the Sun's world, enjoys pleasures long, and then is born on earth as a righteous man, free from disease.
Then by the merit of the vow he gains the vow again, and by that merit, piercing the Sun's orb, O best of brahmins,
he attains Brahman, stainless, formless and beyond the pairs. Here too is declared the vow called Akhanda, O best of brahmins:
making a golden image called Janardana and worshipping it with perfumes, flowers and the like, one should feed brahmins before it,
twelve every month, eating only at night with senses controlled; then at the end of the year, worshipping the image duly,
one should give it with a cow to the teacher and pray thus: "Whatever unbroken vow I have kept in a hundred births,
O Lord, by your grace may it be unbroken for me here." Then feeding the best brahmins with milk-rice rich with sugar,
one should give twelve golden fees and bow. Having kept this vow, O brahmin, and pleased Janardana,
one goes in a golden celestial car to Vishnu's supreme abode. On the twelfth of the dark half of Pausha the Rupa vow is declared:
on the tenth, having bathed duly, the vow-keeper should take cow dung, of a white or single-coloured cow, caught before it touches the ground, O brahmin,
and making a hundred and eight balls of it, O Narada, dry them in the sun, placing them in a copper or earthen vessel.
On the eleventh, fasting and duly worshipping a golden image of Vishnu, one should keep vigil at night
with auspicious songs and music, recitations of hymns, japa and the like; then at dawn on the twelfth, placing the image, set on a vessel of sesame,
on a pitcher full of water, one should worship it with offerings; then producing a new fire by rubbing sticks and the like,
and worshipping it duly, the wise one should offer the balls one by one with sesame and ghee, with the twelve-syllable vidya
or the Vaishnava mantra, and the full oblation, a hundred and eight; then with a loving heart feed brahmins with milk-rice,
and give the image with the pitcher to the teacher; giving fees to brahmins according to one's means, bowing, one should dismiss them. Man or woman, keeping this vow with reverence,
gains beauty and good fortune; there is no doubt. In the bright half of Sahasya is the Sujanma Dvadashi vow:
having bathed duly, one should take up the year-long vow, first drinking water from a cow's horn and circumambulating the cow;
then every month on the bright twelfth one should give: a prastha of ghee, four prasthas of rice, of barley in turn,
two rattis of gold, half an adhaka of sesame, a pitcher of milk, one masha of silver, satisfying sweet cooked food,
an umbrella, half a masha of gold, a prastha of excellent treacle, a pala of sandal, and a fine cloth five cubits long;
making these monthly gifts, one should take in order cow's urine, water or ghee, the four kinds of cooked vegetables,
barley food with curd, sesame and ghee with sugar, and water with darbha and milk — the monthly things to be taken.
Having kept the vow thus for a year, making a golden image of the Sun, placing it on a copper vessel and duly worshipping it,
one should give it with a cow to the teacher and bow before him; feeding twelve brahmins, one should give them fees.
Having kept this vow, O brahmin, one gains birth in an excellent family, healthy, rich in wealth and grain, with unimpaired senses.
On the twelfth of the bright half of Magha, O brahmin, worshipping a shalagrama stone duly with devotion, one should place gold in its mouth,
set it in a silver vessel covered with a pair of white cloths, give it to a knower of the Veda, and then feed him
with wholesome milk-rice with sugar and ghee. Having done so, eating once and intent on meditating on Vishnu,
one gains Vishnu's abode after enjoying desired pleasures here. On the bright twelfth of the last month, a golden image of Hari,
worshipped with perfumes, flowers and the like, should be given to a knower of the Veda, O brahmin; feeding twelve brahmins and giving fees,
one should dismiss them and then eat with one's kin. Trisprisha, Unmilini, Pakshavardhini and Vanjuli,
Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanti and Aparajita — these eight twelfths, removers of sin, should always be fasted on.
Shri Narada said: "What are their characteristics, O Brahman, and what their fruit? Tell me all of it, and of any others that give merit."
Suta said: Asked thus by Narada, the excellent brahmin Sanatana praised his brother and spoke to the great devotee of the Lord.
Sanatana said: "Well asked, brother, you who cut away the doubts of the good. I will tell you separately the characteristics and fruit of the great twelfths.
If the eleventh ends before sunrise, then the twelfth is called Trisprisha, of great fruit;
whoever, fasting on it, worships Govinda, O Narada, surely gains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
When the eleventh is touched by the tenth at dawn, one should give it up and fast on the twelfth;
worshipping there the one called Vasudeva properly with the procedure of worship, one gains on the Unmilita the fruit of a thousand Rajasuyas.
When at sunrise the twelfth touches the eleventh, then one should always give that up and fast on the one called Vanjulika;
on it one should constantly worship with devotion the god Sankarshana, supreme giver of fearlessness to all, with perfumes and other offerings.
This great twelfth grants the fruit of all sacrifices, is declared to remove all sins and grants all prosperity.
When the new-moon and full-moon days are extended, O brahmin, then the twelfth is called Pakshavardhini, of great fruit;
on it one should worship the god Pradyumna, lord of the worlds, granting all lordship and increasing sons and grandsons.
When in the bright fortnight the twelfth falls with Magha, it is called Jaya, destroyer of all enemies;
on it one should worship the god Aniruddha, lord of Rama, who grants men all desires and all good fortune.
If the twelfth in the bright fortnight falls with the constellation Shravana, it is called Vijaya; on it one should worship Gadadhara,
who always grants all happiness and is intent on all enjoyments; fasting on it, O brahmin, a man gains the fruit of all tirthas.
When in the bright fortnight it falls with the constellation of Prajapati, that twelfth is most holy and remembered by the name Jayanti;
on it one should worship the god Vamana, who grants men success; fasted on, O best of brahmins, it grants the fruit of all vows,
the fruit of all gifts, and enjoyment and liberation. When in the bright fortnight the twelfth falls with the constellation of Jupiter,
it is called Aparajita, granting all knowledge; on it one should worship the god Narayana, free from ill,
the ocean of knowledge who cuts the bonds of worldly existence; merely by fasting on it one is freed, O brahmin, by feeding [brahmins].
When on the bright twelfth of Ashadha the constellation Anuradha falls, two vows are to be kept; there is no fault, since the deity is one.
On the twelfth of the bright half of Bhadra with Shravana, and on the bright twelfth of Urja with Revati, two vows as well.
Apart from these, O best of brahmins, on the twelfth a single meal is naturally prescribed — a vow that destroys sins.
Since the vow of the eleventh is perpetual together with the twelfth, no concluding rite is prescribed here; it should be kept for life."
Then every month on the thirteenth of the bright fortnight the vow should be kept in the same way; at the end of the year one should give an adorned cow
to a brahmin with honour, for the completeness of the vow. On the thirteenth of the bright half of Jyeshtha is the vow that quells misfortune:
bathing in river water, one should worship a white mandara, an arka or a red oleander growing in a clean place;
looking at the sun in the sky, one should then pray with a mantra: "Mandara, oleander and arka, you are born of the Sun's portion;
worshipped, may you destroy my misfortune; salutations to you." Whoever worships the three trees with devotion thus year after year,
his misfortune perishes; there is no doubt. On the thirteenth of the bright half of Shuchi one should keep one meal,
worshipping the Lords of the world, the forms of Uma and Maheshvara, made of gold, silver or clay according to one's means,
installing them seated on lion and bull in a temple, a cowshed or a brahmin's house, and consecrating them with the divine mantra, O Narada;
then for five days worship and the vow of one meal; on the third day, in the morning, having bathed and worshipped them again,
one should give them to a brahmin versed in the Vedas and their limbs; thereafter it should be done year after year for five years,
and at the end one should give them with a pair of cows. Man or woman, keeping this auspicious vow,
never suffers separation of husband and wife in seven births. On the thirteenth of the bright half of Nabhas is the auspicious Ratikama vow,
averting widowhood for women and increasing offspring: a maiden or a woman who has fasted, O best of brahmins,
placing Rati and Kama in copper, clay, gold or silver, should worship them well with perfumes and the like;
then on the fourteenth, inviting a brahmin couple, honouring and feeding them, she should give them the images with fees.
Having kept this unsurpassed vow thus for fourteen years, they should be given with a pair of cows for the completion of the vow.
On the thirteenth of the bright half of Bhadra is remembered the Gotriratra vow: making a Lakshmi-Narayana of gold or silver,
bathing it with the five nectars, placing it clothed on a seat in an auspicious eight-petalled mandala, one should worship it with perfumes and the like,
then wave lights and give a pitcher of water with food. Doing this for three days, and at the end of the vow worshipping for a month,
and properly arranging the arghya, one should give it with a mantra, O Narada: "Five cows arose when the great ocean was churned;
among them the one that is Nanda — to that cow, salutations again and again." Then circumambulating, one should give her to a brahmin with a mantra:
May cows be before me, may cows be behind me, may cows be at my sides; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Then worshipping a brahmin couple properly, one should feed them and, honouring him, give him the Lakshmi-Narayana.
Whatever fruit one gains by performing a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rajasuyas, that comes from the Gotriratra vow.
On the thirteenth of the bright half of Isha is the three-night Ashoka vow: making a golden ashoka and worshipping it duly,
the woman intent on fasting should daily make a hundred and eight circumambulations, O brahmin, with reverence, with this mantra:
O Ashoka, you were made long ago by compassionate Hara as a benefactor of the world; be gracious, beloved of Shiva.
Then on the third day, worshipping the bull-bannered god at that tree duly, and feeding a brahmin, she should give it.
A woman who keeps this vow never meets widowhood; with sons, grandsons and the rest she becomes very dear to her husband.
On the thirteenth of the dark half of Urja, eating once and collected, at dusk lighting an oil lamp and worshipping it carefully,
one should place it outside the house door, saying, "May Yama be pleased with me." When this is done, O best of brahmins, affliction from Yama does not arise.
On the thirteenth of the bright half of Urja, eating once, O best of brahmins, bathing again at dusk, silent and collected,
one should illumine Shiva with a thousand lamps, or a hundred, O brahmin, or with a garland of thirty-two lamps;
one should light the lamps with ghee and worship Shiva with perfumes and the like, with various fruits and food offerings, O Narada,
and then praise the Lord of gods, Shiva, with a hundred names; those names, which grant all wishes, are now told:
Salutations to Rudra, Bhima, Nilakantha, the Creator, the one with matted locks, lord of gods, whose hair is the sky;
salutations to the bull-bannered one, Soma, Somanatha; to the naked one, Bhringa, beloved of Uma, the one who increases;
salutations to the one made of austerity, the pervading one, Shipivishta; salutations to the lover of serpents, the serpent, the lord of serpents;
salutations to the upholder of the earth, the sky, the lord of creatures; to the slayer of Tripura, the lion, the tiger, the bull;
salutations to the measured one, lord of the measured, the perfected, the Supreme; to the one sung in the Veda, the hidden one, the secret of the Veda;
to the long, the one of long form, the one of long meaning, the greater; salutations to the foundation of the world, the one whose form is the sky;
to the auspicious, the distinguished, the disciplined, the Supreme Self; to the wearer of the elephant hide, the one who pierced the asura Andhaka;
to the blue-red and white one, the lover of Chanda and Munda, the god who loves devotion, the end of sacrifice, the imperishable;
salutations to you, Mahesha, Mahadeva, Hara; to the three-eyed, the three Vedas, the limbs of the Veda, salutations again and again;
salutations to the aim, the form of aims, the supreme aim; salutations to the universal form, the universe, the lord of the universe;
to Shankara, Kala, the one whose form is the parts of time; salutations to the formless, the misshapen, the subtlest of the subtle;
to you who dwell in the cremation ground, salutations to you clad in hide; to the moon-crested one, who dwells in Rudra's land;
to Durga, the one beyond difficulties, the witness of Durga's limbs; salutations to the one in linga form, the linga, the lord of lingas;
salutations to the one whose form is power, salutations to the one whose meaning is power;
salutations again and again to you, cause of causes, Mrityunjaya, whose form is self-born; to Tryambaka, blue-throated, of Bhrigu's line, joined with Gauri, the cause of good — salutations.
Having recited this hundred names, O brahmin, a celebration of the Pinaka-bearer's virtues, and circumambulating, one should go to one's own home.
Having kept this vow, O brahmin, by Mahadeva's grace one enjoys all pleasures here and at the end gains Shiva's abode.
On the thirteenth of the bright half of Margashirsha, whoever duly worships Ananga, born of union with Shiva, three times or once a day,
worshipping with perfumes and other offerings duly, on a pitcher or an auspicious cloth, should feed a brahmin couple,
then give a fee and eat once himself. When this is done duly, the vow-keeper becomes a vessel of good fortune on earth, O best of brahmins, by Mahadeva's grace.
On the thirteenth of the bright half of Pausha, worshipping Hari, Achyuta, one should give a vessel of ghee to an excellent brahmin for all success.
Beginning from the thirteenth of the bright half of Magha, for three days, the vow of bathing in Magha brings the fruit of many desires, O brahmin.
The fruit of one who bathes three days at Prayaga in the month of Magha is not gained on earth even by a thousand horse-sacrifices;
bathing, japa, oblation and giving there become endless. In the bright half of Phalguna, fasting on the thirteenth,
bowing to the Lord of the world, one should begin the Dhanada vow: the great king, lord of the Yakshas, with perfumes and other offerings,
drawn in colours on a cloth, should be worshipped with devotion; thus on the bright thirteenth every month, O best of brahmins,
a man should worship, fasting or eating once; then at the end of the vow, again making a golden lord of wealth
with golden treasures, O best of brahmins, with the sixteen offerings, bathing with the five nectars and the like,
and various food offerings, one should worship with devotion and concentration; then adorning a cow with clothes, garlands, perfumes and ornaments,
one should have the auspicious cow with its calf given to a proper knower of the Veda, O brahmin; feeding twelve or thirteen brahmins with sweet food,
honouring the teacher with clothes and the like, one should give him that image; giving fees to the brahmins according to one's means, bowing and dismissing them,
the wise one should eat with loved ones, collected. When this vow is kept, O brahmin, a poor man gains wealth
and rejoices on earth, famous like a second king of kings.
Having prayed thus to the Lord of gods, the vow-keeper should sleep on the bare ground, with senses conquered, anger conquered and all enjoyments given up.
Whoever keeps this excellent vow duly, O brahmin, year after year, having enjoyed pleasures, gains Hari's abode.
A pilgrimage to Omkareshvara should also be made here, O lord of sages; worship there is rare, and its sight destroys sin.
What need of more words? Whatever worship, meditation, japa and seeing takes place there is declared to grant men knowledge and liberation.
Here too the linga vow, destroying sin, should be kept: bathing the linga with the five nectars and smearing it with saffron,
with food offerings, fruits, incense, lamps, clothes and ornaments — whoever worships a linga of flour thus, which grants all aims,
gains enjoyment and liberation by Mahadeva's grace. On the fourteenth of the bright half of Jyeshtha, the five fires by day, [water] at night,
and one should give a golden cow at the end — this is remembered as the Rudra vow. On the fourteenth of the bright half of Shuchi a man who worships Shiva
with flowers of the place and season gains all prosperity. On the fourteenth of the bright half of Nabhas the offering of the sacred thread is held;
it should be done by the procedure of one's own Vedic branch, O best of brahmins; consecrating it a hundred times, one should offer it to the Goddess.
A man or woman who performs the offering of the sacred thread gains enjoyment and liberation by the grace of the great Goddess.
On the fourteenth of the bright half of Bhadra is the excellent Ananta vow: one should eat once; cooking a cake of a prastha of wheat flour
smeared with sugar and ghee, one should offer it to Ananta, first worshipping with perfumes and the like; of cotton or silk
making a beautiful thread with fourteen knots, then taking off the old thread and casting it into a body of water,
a woman should tie the new one on the left arm and a man on the right; cooking the flour cake, one should give it with a fee,
and eat an equal amount oneself — so should one keep this excellent vow for fourteen years, and then the wise should perform the concluding rite:
drawing a sarvatobhadra mandala with coloured grains, one should place on it a beautiful copper pitcher, O sage,
and on it place an auspicious golden image of Ananta covered with yellow silk, and worship it there duly;
one should worship Ganesha, the Mothers, the planets and the world-guardians separately, then perform an oblation with havis and make the full oblation;
a bed with its furnishings, a cow and the image, O best of brahmins, one should give to the teacher with devotion, and feed fourteen other brahmins
with sweet cooked food and please them with fees. Whoever keeps the Ananta vow thus with reverence
becomes a sharer in enjoyment and liberation by Ananta's grace. Here is also the Kadali vow; hear its procedure from me:
man or woman, having bathed, should worship a banana plant in a grove with perfumes, flowers, sprouted grain and the like,
with curd, durva, unbroken rice, lamps, clothes and heaps of cooked food; having worshipped thus with a mantra, the vow-keeper should pray:
O you worshipped by Apsaras, daughters of the gods and daughters of the Nagas, grant health and beauty of body, Goddess; salutations to you.
Having prayed thus, one should feed four maidens or married women adorned with parrot-green, vermilion, collyrium and lac,
bow, complete the rule and go home. When this vow is kept, O brahmin, one gains excellent good fortune
in this world, and goes by celestial car to the supreme heaven. On the fourteenth of the dark half of Isha, for those killed by poison, weapons, water or fire,
by snakes, beasts, lightning and the like, and for brahmin-slayers, a shraddha should be performed on the fourteenth by the ekoddishta procedure;
one should feed a group of brahmins with sweet cooked food, offer libations, a mouthful to cows and bali to dogs and crows,
then sip water and eat afterwards with one's kin. Whoever performs thus the shraddha with full fees, O brahmin,
lifts up his ancestors and goes to the eternal world of the gods. On the fourteenth of the bright half of Isha, O best of brahmins, worshipping Dharmaraja
properly with perfumes and the like, feeding a brahmin and giving him a golden [image], Dharmaraja protects one on earth, O Narada.
Whoever makes this excellent gift of Dharma's image enjoys excellent pleasures here and goes to heaven at Dharma's command.
On the fourteenth of the dark half of Urja, at moonrise, anointing oneself with oil and bathing, one should worship Dharma and gain freedom from fear of hell.
At dusk one should light oil lamps to please Yama, at a crossroads or outside the house, with concentration.
In the year called Hemalambi, in the glorious month of Kartika, on the fourteenth of the bright half, toward dawn,
the god Vishveshvara, having bathed with the gods at the Manikarnika tirtha, O lord of sages, bearing the triple mark of ash,
himself worshipped himself and performed the Pashupata vow; so there one should perform great worship of the linga with perfumes and the like,
with drona flowers, bilva leaves, arka flowers, ketaka, flowers, fruits, sweet cooked food and various food offerings.
Keeping thus with one meal the vow that pleases Vishvesha, one gains the desires one wishes here and hereafter, O Narada.
Here too the Brahmakurcha vow should be kept by one desiring prosperity: fasting, with senses controlled, one should drink the five cow products at night —
urine of a tawny cow, dung of a black cow, milk declared of a white cow, curd of a red cow,
and ghee taken from a spotted cow, mixed together; then in the morning, bathing with kusha water and satisfying the deities,
and pleasing brahmins, one should eat in silence. This Brahmakurcha vow destroys all sins;
whatever sin was done in childhood, youth or old age perishes at once by the Brahmakurcha fast.
Here too the Pashana vow is declared; hear it, Narada: fasting by day, at night, worshipping Gauri with perfumes and the like, one should offer cakes shaped like stones cooked in ghee.
Having kept this vow as described, O best of brahmins,
a man gains lordship, happiness, good fortune and beauty. On the fourteenth of the bright half of Margashirsha, having eaten once the day before,
fasting, one should worship a golden bull and give it to a brahmin; on the next day, rising in the morning and bathing, one should worship Maheshvara with Uma
with lotus flowers, perfumes, garlands and unguents, feed brahmins with sweet food and please them with fees and the like.
This Shiva vow, O brahmin, grants enjoyment and liberation to those who keep it, teach it, help and approve.
On the fourteenth of the bright half of Pausha is remembered the Virupaksha vow: thinking, "Here I shall gain the presence of Kapardishvara,"
bathing in deep water, O brahmin, one should worship Shiva as Virupaksha with perfumes, garlands, salutations, incense, lamps and abundant food,
and giving what is there to a brahmin, one rejoices in heaven like a god. On the fourteenth of the dark half of Magha libations to Yama are prescribed:
at the time before sunrise, having bathed, one should offer libations to Yama with the fourteen names declared, for release from all sins;
the libation should be made with sesame, darbha and water, and brahmins fed; one should also eat krishara food oneself, in silence.
On the fourteenth of the dark half of the last month is the Shivaratri vow, O brahmin: fasting without water, one should worship day and night
a self-manifest or other linga, or one of earth, with concentration, with perfumes and other offerings, with water, bilva leaves and the like,
with incense, lamps, food offerings, recitations of hymns, japa and the like; then on the next day, worshipping again with offerings,
feeding brahmins with sweet food, one should dismiss them with fees. A mortal who keeps this vow, by Mahadeva's grace,
gains immortal enjoyments, well honoured by the gods. On the fourteenth of the bright half of the last month, worshipping Durga with devotion
with perfumes and other offerings, one should then feed brahmins; having kept this vow of Durga with one meal, O brahmin,
one gains the desires one wishes, here and hereafter, O Narada. On the fourteenth of the dark half of Chaitra, having fasted,
by drinking the water of Kedara one gains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice. For the concluding rite of all of them a general procedure is declared:
fourteen pitchers here, with betel nut, unbroken rice and modakas, with fees and cloths, of copper or clay, new and undamaged,
as many bamboo staffs, pavitras, seats, vessels and sacred threads should be prepared;
the rest one should do as described before, free from stinginess with wealth.
Two golden images of Uma and Mahesha, and fifteen excellent pitchers of gold, silver or clay —
in one pitcher the two clothed images should be placed; bathing them with the five nectars and then with pure water, one should worship them
with the sixteen offerings; then one should feed fifteen brahmins with sweet food and give them fees,
and give each pitcher of the Lord, with the image, to the teacher. Having kept thus the vow called Umamaheshvara,
one becomes famous on earth, a treasury of all riches. On this same day the Shakra vow is also remembered.
